Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes

Hong-Ye Hu Thanks: hongyehu@iphy.ac.cn, txiang@iphy.ac.cn, chenzhao@eitech.edu.cn Affiliation: Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100910, China    Zhenlai Wang Affiliation: Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100910, China    Binzhao Luo Affiliation: Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100910, China    Tao Xiang Thanks: hongyehu@iphy.ac.cn, txiang@iphy.ac.cn, chenzhao@eitech.edu.cn Affiliation: Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100910, China Affiliation: School of Physical Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China    Chen Zhao Thanks: hongyehu@iphy.ac.cn, txiang@iphy.ac.cn, chenzhao@eitech.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo, Zhejiang 315200, China
Abstract

Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have emerged as a promising approach to reducing the substantial physical qubit overhead of quantum error correction, enabling encoding rates exceeding 1/21/2 in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits. However, their practical implementation requires decoders that combine high accuracy with low latency to keep pace with quantum hardware. Existing decoders of high-rate qLDPC codes can achieve high accuracy but often incur substantial computational latency, whereas neural network decoders have yet to be demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes. Here, we introduce neural triage decoding, a framework that uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation. A local neural message-passing network rapidly predicts error corrections, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections to the remaining shots. We demonstrate that the Triage decoder can decode ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to the near optimal algorithmic decoders while reducing decoding latency by approximately one to two orders of magnitude. Our framework is inspired by a rigorous analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, revealing a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor. In addition, we show the robustness of neural network decoders to mismatched error priors. Our results establish adaptive neural decoding as a promising route towards fast, accurate, and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.

I Introduction

Quantum error correction (QEC), which protects quantum information through redundant encoding, is central to building a fault-tolerant quantum computer [71, 74, 33]. Recent experiments have demonstrated error suppression and key components of QEC on superconducting processors [44, 32, 31], neutral-atom platforms [10, 11], and trapped-ion systems [22, 69, 65], marking substantial progress towards fault-tolerant quantum computation. Scaling these advances to practical quantum algorithms [72, 50, 3, 35, 37] requires sufficiently low logical error rates at a manageable physical-qubit cost [27, 28, 80, 8, 15]. Recent developments in high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes offer a route to reducing this cost by encoding many logical qubits within a single block while retaining sparse parity checks [14, 34, 81, 9, 76, 63, 48, 13, 42]. In particular, codes with encoding rates exceeding one half can accommodate hundreds of logical qubits in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits, substantially reducing the encoding overhead [85, 42, 47, 82, 51, 61]. Realizing this advantage also requires a fast and accurate classical decoder that infers corrections to logical observables from measured syndromes. Decoding accuracy determines how effectively the code suppresses logical errors, while sustained throughput must keep pace with syndrome generation and latency must meet the timing requirements of logical feedback [24, 75, 31].

Exact decoding is computationally challenging, and finding an optimal correction is NP-hard even for general classical codes [7]. Quantum degeneracy adds a further computational challenge, making optimal decoding of stabilizer codes #\#P-complete [41]. Practical decoders must therefore balance accuracy, speed, and versatility. Belief propagation (BP) is a natural choice for qLDPC codes because it exploits their sparse parity checks, supports parallel computation, and achieves near-optimal performance for classical LDPC codes [25, 45, 19]. In quantum codes, however, degeneracy and short cycles can prevent BP from converging, leaving corrections that do not reproduce the measured syndrome [54, 66, 52]. These difficulties have motivated BP variants such as relay-BP [56], as well as post-processing methods that supplement BP with ordered statistics decoding (OSD) [23, 62, 67], localized statistics decoding (LSD) [39], or search-based correction [85, 1, 83, 16]. Such approaches can substantially improve accuracy and, in some settings, achieve near-optimal decoding performance [85]. Their computational cost, particularly for most-likely-error (MLE) search, nevertheless remains a barrier to the high throughput required for real-time decoding.

Neural networks offer another route to the versatile, accurate and fast decoder envisioned in Figure 1(a) [77, 55, 70]. They can learn directly from experimental data and adapt to device-specific noise [4, 6, 46]. Autoregressive and transformer models can capture global correlations and approach optimal decoding, but often at substantial computational cost [17, 6, 12]. On the other hand, architectures such as Cascade neural decoders exploit code symmetries to achieve fast and accurate decoding for specific code families [36] and the performance for high-rate qLDPC codes is unclear. Graph neural networks (GNNs) offer broader applicability by using Tanner graphs as a common representation while retaining the sparse, parallel message passing of BP [49, 29, 57, 53]. However, like BP, they can fail to produce syndrome-consistent corrections [29]; whether they can match the strongest algorithmic decoders across different code families remains unclear. Although neural qLDPC decoders have been demonstrated on blocks encoding tens of logical qubits [57, 53], their performance on ultra-high-rate codes encoding hundreds of logical qubits per block remains unestablished. This regime demands accurate inference over a vast space of logical outcomes: a block encoding 500 logical qubits has 2500≈101502^{500}\approx 10^{150} logical classes in a single code block.

In this work, we introduce Neural Triage Decoding (Triage), a versatile, fast, and accurate neural decoder that extends the idea of a local decoder through iterative decoding and adaptive search for syndrome-consistent corrections (see Figure 1 (a)). Its core graph-based message-passing decoder (NeuralMP) predicts physical corrections through local updates on the sparse Tanner graph of a detector error model (DEM). Within each message-passing round (MP-round), updates to nodes of the same type can be evaluated in parallel, making neural inference well suited to GPU execution. Then it outputs a marginal likelihood of error on each error node. We also show the limitations of bitwise marginal decoding and propose iterative decoding through virtual updates on the syndromes, shown as the second step in Figure 1 (b). If a syndrome compatible solution is still not reached, we invoke the last stage of diversification, which combines syndrome flips [79], perturbation of the prior distribution [66], and symmetric permutation [43]. The diversification reuses the same trained neural network as a general strategy to resolve syndrome-error compatibility without retraining.

We evaluate Triage’s performance on the high-rate lifted-product (LP) code [[1122,148,d≤20]][[1122,148,d\leq 20]] (LP20) [15] and ultra-high-rate Kasai code [[1152,580,d≤12]][[1152,580,d\leq 12]] [42, 85] with phenomenological error models across rr noisy measurement rounds, with a final perfect syndrome extraction. These two codes are representative of product-based and non-product-based constructions of high-rate qLDPC codes, respectively. While being versatile, Triage achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) decoding accuracy that is comparable to or better than that of algorithmic decoders, such as BP-OSD and BP-relay-MLE (Tiered) [85], achieving a per-qubit-per-round error rate of around 5×10−105\times 10^{-10} at p=1.5%p=1.5\% physical error rate on the Kasai code (Figure 1d). Alongside this accuracy, Triage reduces decoding latency and increases throughput by factors of 1010-100100 relative to algorithmic decoders (Figure 1d). Triage thus brings versatility, accuracy, and speed together in a common framework for decoding ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes. With further hardware optimization, this framework offers a path towards real-time error correction of hundreds of logical qubits within a single code block.

II Results

Local marginal decoder and iterative decoding

We formulate decoding using a detector error model with FF fault mechanisms and mm detectors. A fault configuration e→\vec{e} produces a syndrome s→=H​e→\vec{s}=H\vec{e} and logical-observable flips ℓ=L​e→\bm{\ell}=L\vec{e}, with arithmetic over GF⁡(2)\mathrm{GF}(2). NeuralMP predicts one score per fault mechanism by passing messages on the sparse bipartite graph defined by HH [57], which is also called the Tanner graph. Syndrome values svs_{v} and mechanism priors pfp_{f} are encoded as χ\chi-dimensional detector and fault states, shown as colored bars in Figure 2(a), with learned coordinate embeddings supplying positional information. Each of RR MP-rounds first updates fault states using detector states, then updates detector states using the updated fault states (Figure 2(b)). Trainable functions Fθv→fF_{\theta}^{v\to f} and Fθ′f→vF_{\theta^{\prime}}^{f\to v} combine each node’s current state with the sum of its incoming messages. Parameters are shared across nodes of each type within an MP-round, enabling parallel updates, but differ between MP-rounds. A linear readout of the final fault states gives logits zfz_{f} and learned fault scores qf=σ⁡(zf)q_{f}=\sigma(z_{f}), where σ⁡(x)=(1+e−x)−1\sigma(x)=(1+e^{-x})^{-1} is the sigmoid function. Crucially, for N=m+FN=m+F nodes and EE edges, one evaluation costs 𝒪⁡(R⁡[E​χ+N​χ2])\mathcal{O}(R[E\chi+N\chi^{2}]), which is linear in NN when E=𝒪⁡(N)E=\mathcal{O}(N) at fixed R,χR,\chi. In contrast, the global decoders that use attention mechanism will have costs that scale as 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) [78].

During training, the Triage decoder readily learns to correct common error patterns, but rare and difficult decoding cases are the important ones determining its performance in the low error rate regime. To enhance the sparse training reward, we couple online error-weight-conditioned simulation with a dynamically updated mistake bank (Figure 2(c)). We store hard decoding examples in the online mistake bank and remove them from the bank after repeated successes. We also augment replayed examples using code symmetries, jointly permuting fault patterns and syndromes. This failure-aware loop combines targeted data generation with the supervision of fault predictions, logical observables, and syndrome consistency. Implementation details are provided in the Methods.

Independent decisions from marginal probabilities can violate syndrome constraints even when the marginals are exact. To illustrate the ambiguity, consider independent ZZ noise on nn qubits of a Calderbank–Shor–Steane (CSS) code and an even-weight ZZ stabilizer gg of weight ww. Errors eAe_{A} and eB=eA⊕ge_{B}=e_{A}\oplus g occupying complementary halves of its support both have weight w/2w/2. Since H​g=0Hg=0 and L​g=0Lg=0, they share the same syndrome and logical labels. Either specified error, with no other errors, occurs with probability pw/2​(1−p)n−w/2=Θ⁡(pw/2)p^{w/2}(1-p)^{n-w/2}=\Theta(p^{w/2}). If this pair gives the only minimum-weight explanations of its syndrome, each supported qubit has an exact posterior marginal approaching 1/21/2 as p→0p\to 0. Such local ambiguities can arise from stabilizers whose weight does not grow with code distance. In phenomenological noise models, space–time degeneracies involving both data and measurement errors can have lower weight than purely spatial stabilizers.

Theorem 1 (Syndrome inconsistency under phenomenological noise).

Consider a CSS code with Z-check matrix HZH_{Z} of minimum qubit degree ν≥2\nu\geq 2, with no 4-cycles in its Tanner graph and no nonzero kernel vector of weight below 2​ν+22\nu+2. In the independent X/ZX/Z phenomenological model defined in Methods, with r≥5r\geq 5 noisy measurement rounds, data error rate pp, and measurement error rate q=Θ⁡(p)q=\Theta(p), the exact bitwise marginal decoder, using maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decisions, satisfies

Pinc​(p):=Pr⁡(H​e^≠H​e)\displaystyle P_{\mathrm{inc}}(p):=\Pr(H\hat e\ne He) =Ω(pκ⁡(ν))(p→0),\displaystyle=\Omega(p^{\kappa(\nu)})\qquad(p\to 0), (1)
κ⁡(ν)\displaystyle\kappa(\nu) ={ν/2+1,ν​ even,ν+1,ν​ odd.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\nu/2+1,&\nu\text{ even},\\ \nu+1,&\nu\text{ odd}.\end{cases}

The LP and Kasai code shots used here have ν=3\nu=3, so Theorem 1 yields Pinc​(p)=Ω⁡(p4)P_{\mathrm{inc}}(p)=\Omega(p^{4}) for their independent X/ZX/Z phenomenological models. Single-pass NeuralMP results are consistent with this mechanism (Figure 2(d)). The proof and finite-instance certificates are given in the Methods and the Supplementary Information.

Motivated by this understanding, we propose the idea of iterative decoding, which addresses residual violations by repeatedly applying the same trained network to the current residual syndrome (Figure 1(b)). Starting from e^(0)=0\hat{e}^{(0)}=0 and 𝒔res(0)=s\bm{s}_{\mathrm{res}}^{(0)}=s, each outer iteration kk samples a proposal δ​e(k)\delta e^{(k)} and updates

e^(k+1)\displaystyle\hat{e}^{(k+1)} =e^(k)⊕δ​e(k),\displaystyle=\hat{e}^{(k)}\oplus\delta e^{(k)},
𝒔res(k+1)\displaystyle\bm{s}_{\mathrm{res}}^{(k+1)} =𝒔res(k)⊕H​δ​e(k).\displaystyle=\bm{s}_{\mathrm{res}}^{(k)}\oplus H\delta e^{(k)}. (2)

Decoding stops when the residual vanishes or reaches the maximum KmaxK_{\text{max}} iterations. Practically, we set Kmax=4K_{\text{max}}=4. Shots unresolved after KmaxK_{\text{max}} outer iterations proceed to the final stage of diversification.

Improved convergence with diversification

Residual-guided iteration can be complemented by diversification, which explores alternative correction trajectories under different inference conditions. The relay-BP decoder follows the same principle by varying local memory strengths to diversify BP trajectories [56]. For a fixed neural decoder, we generate alternative correction candidates through prior perturbations, symmetric permutations, and syndrome flips, using information from the decoder to guide the search (see Figure 1 (b)). In particular, near-zero logit outputs identify uncertain error mechanisms, while repeated corrections at the same locations indicate instability along an iterative trajectory.

Each diversification trajectory starts from the original syndrome and reuses the iterative decoder under modified inference conditions. Prior perturbations modify the mechanism priors supplied to the network, shifting its preferences among competing correction proposals. Symmetric permutations preserve the Tanner graph of the DEM and mechanism priors but change the alignment of the syndrome with the network’s coordinate encodings, allowing different predictions that are mapped back to the original coordinates. For syndrome flips, we select a small set of mechanisms, represented by a binary vector t→\vec{t}, using marginal uncertainty and repeated corrections as guides. We apply the iterative decoder to the modified syndrome s→⊕H​t→\vec{s}\oplus H\vec{t} with the original priors, then combine its prediction e′→\vec{e^{\prime}} with t→\vec{t} to obtain the candidate e^=t→⊕e′→\hat{e}=\vec{t}\oplus\vec{e^{\prime}}. The resulting candidates are checked against the original syndrome, and syndrome-consistent candidates are ranked by their negative log-likelihood under the original mechanism priors.

The effect of a syndrome flip can be seen in the half-support issue described above, where two complementary errors a→\vec{a} and b→\vec{b} each have weight w/2w/2 and produce the same syndrome. Choosing t→\vec{t} to contain a single qubit in the support of a→\vec{a} maps these errors to a→⊕t→\vec{a}\oplus\vec{t} and b→⊕t→\vec{b}\oplus\vec{t}, both consistent with the modified syndrome but with weights w/2−1w/2-1 and w/2+1w/2+1, respectively. Under the unchanged independent-error prior with p<1/2p<1/2, the former is more likely by a factor [(1−p)/p]2[(1-p)/p]^{2}. In the two-candidate example, this imbalance moves the marginals away from 1/21/2 and favors a consistent choice, which is then mapped back to a correction for the original syndrome. The flip thus changes the preference between candidates during search without changing their relative likelihood in the original decoding problem.

We organize these diversification strategies into a conditional decoding procedure that allocates additional computation to shots with unresolved syndromes. Shots whose residual syndrome vanishes during the initial iterative stage return immediately, and the remainder enter a syndrome-flip stage guided by marginal uncertainty and repeated corrections. If it produces syndrome-consistent candidates, we return the best candidate according to the selection rule above. Shots with no such candidate can proceed to a supplementary search stage which has further sign flip strategy and symmetric permutations combined with prior perturbations. Predictions from different symmetry-related views are mapped back to the original coordinates, and their disagreement identifies locations for additional syndrome flips. Candidates from this stage are evaluated by the same rule. If the search budget is exhausted without a syndrome-consistent candidate, the decoder retains the correction returned by the initial iterative stage, and the shot remains unresolved.

Decoding high-rate qLDPC codes

We evaluate Triage’s performance on the lifted-product code [[1122,148,≤20]][[1122,148,\leq 20]] and the ultra-high-rate Kasai code [[1152,580,d≤12]][[1152,580,d\leq 12]], spanning encoding rates of 13.2%13.2\% and 50.3%50.3\%, respectively. Both benchmarks use phenomenological noise, with data errors and multiple noisy syndrome measurements followed by a final perfect syndrome extraction. For the LP20 code, we simulate five noisy measurement rounds, with independent XX and ZZ errors, each occurring with probability pp on every data qubit, and measurement outcomes flipped with probability pp. For the Kasai code, we simulate eight noisy measurement rounds under depolarizing noise, with XX, YY, and ZZ errors, each occurring with a probability of p/3p/3, and measurement outcomes flipped with a probability of 4​p/34p/3. For both codes, diversification begins with syndrome flips. For LP20, unresolved shots proceed to an additional stage combining prior perturbations, symmetric permutations, and further syndrome flips guided by disagreement between symmetry-related predictions; Kasai uses only the initial syndrome-flip stage. Crucially, for both LP20 and Kasai codes, we train Triage at a single physical error rate, p=2%p=2\%, and evaluate its performance across a range of previously unseen error rates.

We observe that Triage decoder achieves low logical error rates while substantially reducing amortized decoding costs. For example, at p=0.015p=0.015, its estimated per-qubit-per-round LER is 9.33×10−119.33\times 10^{-11} on LP20 and 5.08×10−105.08\times 10^{-10} on Kasai, compared with 4.43×10−104.43\times 10^{-10} for BP-OSD and 1.76×10−91.76\times 10^{-9} for the BP-relay-MLE Tiered decoder, respectively (see Figure 3 (a)). These accuracies are obtained through iterative NeuralMP decoding with diversification. At the same error rate, the estimated full-decoder costs at batch size 64 are 2.372.37 ms and 12.312.3 ms per shot on a single NVIDIA H-series GPU, compared with CPU baseline means of 815815 ms and 349349 ms for BP-OSD and the Tiered decoder, respectively (see Figure 3 (b)). These benchmark settings yield approximately 343×343\times and 28×28\times speedups.

We further examine its robustness to inaccurate noise calibration by perturbing the priors supplied to the decoder while keeping the physical noise fixed. This is important as the noise distribution can shift from the initial noise learning, and control drifts can also happen during the computation [73, 30]. We perturb the prior error uniform distribution as pf→pf​(1+σr​𝒩​(0,1))p_{f}\rightarrow p_{f}(1+\sigma_{r}\mathcal{N}(0,1)), where 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) is the Gaussian distribution with zero mean and unit variance. We investigate the ratio between the whole block logical error rate with the perturbed prior distribution over that of the original prior distribution. In Figure 4, we show that the four-iteration Triage frontend (NeuralMP) maintains a block-LER ratio close to unity across the tested perturbations. At the largest nominal mismatch strength, σr=0.5\sigma_{r}=0.5, its ratios are approximately 1.011.01 for the LP20 code and 0.980.98 for the Kasai code, whereas the corresponding algorithmic baselines show increases of approximately 1.61.6–2.12.1 times relative to matched-prior decoding. These results suggest that neural-network-based decoders can offer passive resilience to uncertainty and fluctuations in noise parameters, analogous to robust quantum controls [18, 40, 64].

III Discussion

Triage decoder combines a local neural message-passing network with iterative decoding and a rarely invoked diversification to allocate computation according to decoding difficulty. This architecture is inspired by the theoretical understanding of the limitations of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, where there exists a lower bound on the residual syndrome density even when the marginal distribution is exact. The results on lifted-product and Kasai codes show that Triage can achieve SOTA decoding accuracy comparable to and better than that of the algorithmic decoders, with substantially lower amortized decoding costs than the tested algorithmic baselines. In addition, we show the robustness of the Triage decoder against the error prior distribution, which is important and relevant for real-time decoding with hardware fluctuations. These results also suggest several directions for improving the decoder and connecting it to experimental operation.

Symmetric permutations currently enter Triage through diversification. Incorporating these symmetries directly into NeuralMP, for example, through symmetry-respecting parameter sharing as suggested in Cascade [36], could reduce network size and inference cost. The different effectiveness of diversification proposals across the two codes also motivates a more systematic analysis of decoding failures. Relating the response to syndrome flips, prior perturbations, and symmetric permutations to graph structure and degeneracy could reveal which ambiguities each proposal resolves and guide the choice of proposal and computational budget for each shot.

These diagnostics could support recursive self-improvement (RSI) of Triage. Automated discovery of programs and algorithms with language models [68, 58], together with the discovery of learning rules through meta-learning [60], provides precedents for using machine-generated proposals and quantitative feedback to improve computational methods. In this setting, AI agents could analyze decoding failures, propose changes to the architecture, training procedure, or diversification strategy, and evaluate successive revisions against logical error rates and total decoding costs. This feedback loop could reduce manual tuning while retaining explicit accuracy and runtime criteria [2].

Finally, adaptive decoding and hardware self-calibration could form a coupled feedback loop. Neural decoders can be adapted to experimental data [6], while recent experimental and theoretical work shows how syndrome-derived signals can guide control optimization during error correction [73, 30]. Triage could update mechanism priors or selectively retrain NeuralMP as the noise changes, while detection-event statistics guide the recalibration of the underlying controls. The observed resilience of the four-iteration frontend to the tested prior perturbations provides motivation for studying this integration. Establishing its ability to track physical drift would require evaluating the full decoder and calibration loop together, including the cost and stability of online updates.

Extending Triage from phenomenological quantum memory to circuit-level logical gadgets and algorithms [21, 87, 84, 38, 10, 16, 86], or applying it to experimental data, are central next steps. Real-time operation also requires measuring single-shot latency, its distribution, and sustained throughput against the timing requirements of the hardware [31, 70]. Further work is needed to optimize GPU inference and investigate field-programmable gate array (FPGA) deployment of the trained model [59, 20]. The present GPU and CPU comparisons quantify amortized costs under their stated batching and hardware conditions. These further tests would determine whether adaptive neural decoding can sustain both accurate logical protection and efficient feedback during prolonged operation.

IV Methods

IV.1 NeuralMP architecture

The detector error model specifies FF mechanisms, mm detectors, and kk logical observables through H∈{0,1}m×FH\in\{0,1\}^{m\times F}, L∈{0,1}k×FL\in\{0,1\}^{k\times F}, and priors pfp_{f}, with N=m+FN=m+F nodes in a bipartite Tanner graph. Error configurations differing by a vector in ker⁡H∩ker⁡L\ker H\cap\ker L share both syndrome and logical labels. Initial states combine learned node-type and coordinate features; fault states additionally receive a linear projection of log⁡pf\log p_{f}, and detector states receive the encoded binary outcomes. Coordinate features concatenate learned embeddings for individual nodes, followed by a linear projection and a rectified linear unit (ReLU). Messages include a learned source-type bias before summation, and detector aggregation uses the newly updated fault states. Each directional update takes the current state and aggregate as the input to a two-layer MLP with a ReLU hidden activation. Its output is added to the current state and layer-normalized. Distinct update modules are used for the two directions and for successive MP-rounds, with each module applied in parallel across its node family. The deployed Kasai network uses hidden dimension χ=64\chi=64 and R=80R=80 MP-rounds with distinct MP-round-specific parameters.

Fresh training examples mix natural noise with noise conditioned on selected fault weights. Thresholded predictions with incorrect logical observables enter the replay bank. Verified symmetries transform replayed fault patterns and syndromes together, with logical labels recomputed. The three loss terms are defined in the Training objective subsection. Class weighting and modified sampling distributions mean that the scores are not assumed to be calibrated deployment posteriors.

Each outer iteration is an independent forward pass: hidden states are re-initialized from the current residual syndrome and the original priors, and no hidden state or logit is carried over between iterations. Information propagates between iterations only through the residual syndrome. Proposal bits are sampled independently as δ​ef(k)∼Bernoulli⁡[σ⁡(zf(k)/T)]\delta e_{f}^{(k)}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}[\sigma(z_{f}^{(k)}/T)] and accumulated according to Equation 2. Here T>0T>0 is the sampling temperature. The deployed configuration uses T=1T=1, so qf(k)=σ⁡(zf(k))q_{f}^{(k)}=\sigma(z_{f}^{(k)}), and a budget of at most K=4K=4 network evaluations per shot before escalation to diversification. Parameters remain fixed throughout inference.

IV.2 Training objective

We train NeuralMP using physical-error-level, logical, and syndrome supervision. Let qf=σ⁡(zf)q_{f}=\sigma(z_{f}) denote the network output for fault mechanism ff, and let ee, s=H​es=He and ℓ=L​e\bm{\ell}=Le denote the simulated fault pattern, syndrome and logical-observable flips, respectively. All parity operations are over GF⁡(2)\mathrm{GF}(2). The total loss is

ℒ=ℒfault+ℒlogical+ℒsyndrome,\begin{split}\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fault}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{logical}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{syndrome}},\end{split} (3)

with unit coefficients for all three terms.

The fault loss is binary cross-entropy (BCE), with a positive-class weight of eight to compensate for sparse faults:

ℒfault=−1F∑f[8eflogqf+(1−ef)log⁡(1−qf)].\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fault}}=-\frac{1}{F}\sum_{f}\left[8e_{f}\log q_{f}+(1-e_{f})\log(1-q_f)\right].\end{split} (4)

For logical supervision, we construct a differentiable parity estimate under a factorized Bernoulli approximation,

ℓ~j=1−∏f:Lj​f=1(1−2qf)2,ℒlogical=1k​∑jBCE⁡(ℓ~j,ℓj)\begin{split}\widetilde{\ell}_{j}=\frac{1-\prod_{f:L_{jf}=1}(1-2q_{f})}{2},\\ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{logical}}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j}\mathrm{BCE}(\widetilde{\ell}_{j},\ell_{j})\end{split} (5)

The syndrome-consistency penalty similarly compares predicted fault parities with the measured detectors:

ℒsyndrome=1m∑c[1−(−1)sc∏f:Hc​f=1(1−2qf)].\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{syndrome}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{c}\left[1-(-1)^{s_{c}}\prod_{f:H_{cf}=1}(1-2q_{f})\right].\end{split} (6)

Here, FF, kk, and mm are the numbers of fault mechanisms, logical observables, and detectors. These terms encourage accurate fault predictions, correct logical outcomes and syndrome consistency, respectively; exact consistency is checked separately during decoding.

IV.3 Marginal decoding and syndrome inconsistency

We first establish a criterion for marginal decisions to violate a syndrome constraint. We then derive this criterion from the spatial graph and phenomenological noise assumptions of Theorem 1, and verify those assumptions for the simulated shots. Throughout this subsection, H∈𝔽2m×FH\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times F} is fixed and finite, and the error mechanisms are independent with probabilities pf​(p)=Θ​(p)p_{f}(p)=\Theta(p) as p→0p\to 0. The exact posterior marginals are πf​(s)=Pr⁡(ef=1|H​e=s)\pi_{f}(s)=\Pr(e_f=1\mid He=s). Bitwise MAP sets e^f(s)=𝟏{πf(s)>1/2}\hat{e}_{f}(s)=\bm{1}\{\pi_{f}(s)>1/2\}, assigning ties to zero. All matrix operations are over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}. We write Pinc​(p)=Pr⁡(H​e^≠H​e)P_{\mathrm{inc}}(p)=\Pr(H\hat e\ne He).

Lemma 1 (Concentration on minimum-weight explanations).

For a nonzero attainable syndrome s∗s_{*}, let κ\kappa be its minimum compatible error weight, ℳ∗\mathcal{M}_{*} the set of all compatible weight-κ\kappa errors, and U∗U_{*} the union of their supports. Then

Z∗:=Pr⁡(H​e=s∗)\displaystyle Z_{*}:=\Pr(He=s_*) =Θ⁡(pκ),\displaystyle=\Theta(p^{\kappa}), (7)
Pr⁡(e∉ℳ∗|H​e=s∗)\displaystyle\Pr(e\notin\mathcal M_*\mid He=s_*) =O⁡(p).\displaystyle=O(p).

In particular, πf​(s∗)=O⁡(p)\pi_{f}(s_{*})=O(p) for every f∉U∗f\notin U_{*}.

Proof.

Independence and pf​(p)=Θ​(p)p_{f}(p)=\Theta(p) imply that each fixed weight-tt error has probability Θ⁡(pt)\Theta(p^{t}). Since HH is finite, the total probability of the minimum-weight explanations is Θ⁡(pκ)\Theta(p^{\kappa}), while that of all higher-weight compatible errors is O⁡(pκ+1)O(p^{\kappa+1}). Dividing by Z∗Z_{*} proves posterior concentration. An error on a coordinate outside U∗U_{*} can occur only in a higher-weight explanation, giving the marginal bound. ∎

For an equally likely disjoint pair ℳ∗={a,b}\mathcal{M}_{*}=\{a,b\}, this lemma gives πf​(s∗)=1/2+O⁡(p)\pi_{f}(s_{*})=1/2+O(p) on U∗U_{*}. The higher-weight explanations determine the signs of these small shifts, which control the hard decisions.

Lemma 2 (Two-bit marginal shifts).

Fix a syndrome s∗s_{*} with Z∗>0Z_{*}>0 and distinct bits i,ji,j. Define Wu​v​(p)=Pr⁡(H​e=s∗,ei=u,ej=v)W_{uv}(p)=\Pr(He=s_*,e_i=u,e_j=v) for u,v∈{0,1}u,v\in\{0,1\}, Δ=W00−W11\Delta=W_{00}-W_{11}, and δ=W10−W01\delta=W_{10}-W_{01}. Then

πi​(s∗)−12\displaystyle\pi_{i}(s_{*})-\tfrac{1}{2} =−Δ+δ2​Z∗,\displaystyle=\frac{-\Delta+\delta}{2Z_{*}}, (8)
πj​(s∗)−12\displaystyle\pi_{j}(s_{*})-\tfrac{1}{2} =−Δ−δ2​Z∗.\displaystyle=\frac{-\Delta-\delta}{2Z_{*}}.

The two marginals lie strictly on the same side of 1/21/2 if and only if |Δ|>|δ||\Delta|>|\delta|. In particular, Δ>|δ|\Delta>|\delta| places both below 1/21/2.

Proof.

Use πi=(W10+W11)/Z∗\pi_{i}=(W_{10}+W_{11})/Z_{*}, πj=(W01+W11)/Z∗\pi_{j}=(W_{01}+W_{11})/Z_{*}, and Z∗=∑u,vWu​vZ_{*}=\sum_{u,v}W_{uv}. Subtracting 1/21/2 gives the identities. Their product is (Δ2−δ2)/(4​Z∗2)(\Delta^{2}-\delta^{2})/(4Z_{*}^{2}), which is positive exactly when the shifts have the same nonzero sign. ∎

Proposition 1 (A two-bit inconsistency criterion).

Under the noise assumptions of this subsection, suppose a nonzero syndrome s∗s_{*} has exactly two minimum-weight explanations a,ba,b of weight κ\kappa with disjoint supports, and set U=supp⁡(a⊕b)U=\operatorname{supp}(a\oplus b). Suppose every compatible error supported on UU obeys ei⊕ej=1e_{i}\oplus e_{j}=1 for fixed distinct bits i,j∈Ui,j\in U. If |Δ|>|δ||\Delta|>|\delta| for these bits at all sufficiently small p>0p>0, then exact bitwise MAP has Pinc​(p)=Ω⁡(pκ)P_{\mathrm{inc}}(p)=\Omega(p^{\kappa}).

Proof.

By Lemma 1, Z∗=Θ⁡(pκ)Z_{*}=\Theta(p^{\kappa}) and all marginals outside UU are O⁡(p)O(p). Hence the MAP output is supported on UU for sufficiently small pp. Lemma 2 gives equal MAP decisions on i,ji,j, violating the required odd parity. Thus MAP is inconsistent whenever s∗s_{*} is observed, and Pinc​(p)≥Z∗=Θ⁡(pκ)P_{\mathrm{inc}}(p)\geq Z_{*}=\Theta(p^{\kappa}), independently of ties at other coordinates. ∎

The quantities Δ\Delta and δ\delta separate a common shift of the two endpoint marginals from a preference between them: πi+πj=1−Δ/Z∗\pi_{i}+\pi_{j}=1-\Delta/Z_{*} and πi−πj=δ/Z∗\pi_{i}-\pi_{j}=\delta/Z_{*}. The phenomenological construction below gives these two effects a concrete space–time interpretation.

Theorem 1 assumes mutually independent X/ZX/Z data faults (probability pp each) and measurement flips (q=Θ⁡(p)q=\Theta(p)), with known initial syndromes and a perfect final readout after rr noisy measurement rounds. The code and rr are fixed as p→0p\to 0.

Choose a degree-ν\nu qubit v∗v_{*}. A data fault on this qubit can be moved by τ\tau measurement rounds without changing the syndrome if a string of measurement faults joins the two times on each neighboring check. Writing d→t\vec{d}_{t} for its XX fault in measurement round tt and m→h,t\vec{m}_{h,t} for a measurement fault connecting detectors in measurement rounds t,t+1t,t+1 on check hh, this relation is

g→=d→0+d→τ+∑h∈N⁡(v∗)∑t=0τ−1m→h,t,|g→|=2+τ​ν.\vec{g}=\vec{d}_{0}+\vec{d}_{\tau}+\sum_{h\in N(v_{*})}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1}\vec{m}_{h,t},\qquad|\vec{g}|=2+\tau\nu.

Here H​g→=L​g→=0H\vec{g}=L\vec{g}=0. We split U=supp⁡(g→)U=\operatorname{supp}(\vec{g}) into two complementary explanations a,ba,b, each containing one data endpoint and half of the measurement faults. Taking τ=1\tau=1 for even ν\nu and τ=2\tau=2 for odd ν\nu gives weight κ⁡(ν)=1+τ​ν/2\kappa(\nu)=1+\tau\nu/2. The endpoint bits are i=d0i=d_{0} and j=dτj=d_{\tau}: they refer to the same qubit at different times. The two explanations have equal prior probability even when p≠qp\neq q, and contribute equally to W10W_{10} and W01W_{01}.

Higher-weight explanations modify this balance in two ways. Redistributing data faults on v∗v_{*}, with compensating measurement strings, can produce endpoints 0000 or 1111 and hence change Δ\Delta. For ν=3\nu=3, the first such pair uses either one data fault at the intermediate time or data faults at all three times, together with four or two measurement faults, respectively. A data fault beyond the endpoint pair gives an additional 0000 explanation. Moving the construction from the initial boundary into the interior allows this extension on both sides.

The leading 10,0110,01 extensions involve a pair of data faults at adjacent times on a neighboring degree-ν\nu qubit. Together with compensating edges on that qubit’s other checks, this pair replaces an occupied measurement edge. These extensions preserve the original endpoint values 1010 or 0101; unequal numbers of available extensions produce the leading contribution to δ\delta.

For ν=3\nu=3, label the neighboring checks 1,2,31,2,3 and choose

a→\displaystyle\vec{a} =d→0+m→1,0+m→1,1+m→2,1,\displaystyle=\vec{d}_{0}+\vec{m}_{1,0}+\vec{m}_{1,1}+\vec{m}_{2,1}, (9)
b→\displaystyle\vec{b} =d→2+m→2,0+m→3,0+m→3,1.\displaystyle=\vec{d}_{2}+\vec{m}_{2,0}+\vec{m}_{3,0}+\vec{m}_{3,1}.

Their common syndrome activates checks {2,3}\{2,3\}, {2}\{2\}, and {1,2}\{1,2\} in measurement rounds 0,1,20,1,2. More generally, for even ν=2​k\nu=2k, partition the neighboring checks into sets 𝒜,ℬ\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B} of size kk, and take

a→=d→0+∑h∈𝒜m→h,0,b→=d→1+∑h∈ℬm→h,0.\vec{a}=\vec{d}_{0}+\sum_{h\in\mathcal{A}}\vec{m}_{h,0},\qquad\vec{b}=\vec{d}_{1}+\sum_{h\in\mathcal{B}}\vec{m}_{h,0}.

For odd ν=2​k+1\nu=2k+1, partition them into 𝒜,{c},ℬ\mathcal{A},\{c\},\mathcal{B} with |𝒜|=|ℬ|=k|\mathcal{A}|=|\mathcal{B}|=k, and use

a→\displaystyle\vec{a} =d→0+∑h∈𝒜(m→h,0+m→h,1)+m→c,1,\displaystyle=\vec{d}_{0}+\sum_{h\in\mathcal{A}}(\vec{m}_{h,0}+\vec{m}_{h,1})+\vec{m}_{c,1},
b→\displaystyle\vec{b} =d→2+∑h∈ℬ(m→h,0+m→h,1)+m→c,0.\displaystyle=\vec{d}_{2}+\sum_{h\in\mathcal{B}}(\vec{m}_{h,0}+\vec{m}_{h,1})+\vec{m}_{c,0}.

For either degree parity, write s→∗=H​a→=H​b→\vec{s}_{*}=H\vec{a}=H\vec{b}. Summing the detector equations over time requires ei⊕ej=1e_{i}\oplus e_{j}=1 for every compatible correction supported on UU. Once the data endpoint is chosen, the measurement equations fix all remaining bits, so a,ba,b are the only compatible corrections on UU.

The spatial assumptions in Theorem 1 control explanations extending outside UU. The absence of Tanner 4-cycles limits distinct qubits to at most one shared check, while the bound on ker⁡HZ\ker H_{Z} excludes spatial zero-syndrome patterns of weight below 2​ν+22\nu+2, including stabilizers. Together, these conditions establish that a,ba,b are the only minimum-weight explanations and allow the higher-weight contributions to Δ,δ\Delta,\delta to be classified, as stated next and proved in Supplementary Information.

Proposition 2 (Two-rate structure of the phenomenological witnesses).

Under the spatial and measurement-round assumptions of Theorem 1, the constructed a→,b→\vec{a},\vec{b} are the only minimum-weight explanations of s→∗\vec{s}_{*}, with weight κ=κ⁡(ν)\kappa=\kappa(\nu). Each contains one data fault and κ−1\kappa-1 measurement faults, so they remain equally likely for arbitrary p,qp,q. Put x=p/(1−p)x=p/(1-p), y=q/(1−q)y=q/(1-q), and let F0=1+O⁡(p)F_{0}=1+O(p) be the common no-error factor of the selected sector times the probability of zero syndrome in the other sector. +O⁡(pκ+ν+1).\displaystyle+O(p^{\kappa+\nu+1}).

For odd ν\nu, use two placements of the construction: j=0j=0 starts in measurement round zero, while j=1j=1 shifts every fault and detector by one measurement round. Both have the same minimum weight and prior composition. Their endpoint imbalances satisfy

Δj\displaystyle\Delta_{j} =F0[xyν−1(y2−x2)\displaystyle=F_{0}\bigl[xy^{\nu-1}(y^{2}-x^{2}) (11)
+(1+j)xy2​ν]+O(p2​ν+2),\displaystyle+(1+j)xy^{2\nu}\bigr]+O(p^{2\nu+2}),
δj\displaystyle\delta_{j} =2​F0​(NA−NB)​x3​y2​ν−2\displaystyle=2F_{0}(N_{A}-N_{B})x^{3}y^{2\nu-2}

Proof.

In Supplementary Information, it classifies all compatible configurations through weight κ+ν\kappa+\nu, retaining their separate data and measurement counts. The two minimum explanations have odds weight x​yκ−1xy^{\kappa-1}. For even ν\nu, the next configurations comprise one 0000 explanation with one data fault and 3​ν/23\nu/2 measurement faults, and NA,NBN_{A},N_{B} explanations in classes 10,0110,01, each with three data faults and 3​ν/2−23\nu/2-2 measurement faults. This gives Eq. (10).

For odd ν\nu, the weight-(ν+2)(\nu+2) explanations in classes 00,1100,11 have odds weights x​yν+1xy^{\nu+1} and x3​yν−1x^{3}y^{\nu-1}. They need not cancel when p≠qp\neq q. At weight 2​ν+12\nu+1, a single data fault one measurement round beyond the endpoint pair gives a 0000 explanation with odds weight x​y2​νxy^{2\nu}. The boundary placement admits one such fault; the interior placement admits two, one on each side. The 10,0110,01 counts are unchanged by translation and give their stated difference. All omitted configurations have weight at least 2​ν+22\nu+2, so their total probability is O⁡(p2​ν+2)O(p^{2\nu+2}) because q=Θ⁡(p)q=\Theta(p). The independent other sector contributes the same common factor to both placements. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.

Choose any minimum-degree qubit. For odd ν\nu, fix any central check cc. Choose the remaining partition 𝒜,ℬ\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B} to minimize |NA−NB||N_{A}-N_{B}| and orient it so that η=NA−NB≥0\eta=N_{A}-N_{B}\geq 0.

If η>0\eta>0, we show in Supplementary Information that it excludes both compatible outputs on UU. The positive endpoint preference δ\delta excludes bb. For a check in 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the largest nhn_{h}, a negative measurement marginal bias (or a negative sum of two such biases for odd degree) excludes aa. Posterior concentration rejects every bit outside UU, so the boundary syndrome forces inconsistency.

If η=0\eta=0 and ν\nu is even, Eq. (10) gives Δ=Θ⁡(pκ+ν)>0\Delta=\Theta(p^{\kappa+\nu})>0 and δ=O⁡(pκ+ν+1)\delta=O(p^{\kappa+\nu+1}), again forcing inconsistency by Proposition 1.

For η=0\eta=0 and odd ν\nu, subtract the two expansions in Eq. (11):

Δ1−Δ0=F0​x​y2​ν+O⁡(p2​ν+2)=Θ⁡(p2​ν+1).\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{0}=F_{0}xy^{2\nu}+O(p^{2\nu+2})=\Theta(p^{2\nu+1}).

Thus at least one placement satisfies |Δj|≥|Δ1−Δ0|/2=Ω⁡(p2​ν+1)|\Delta_{j}|\geq|\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{0}|/2=\Omega(p^{2\nu+1}), whereas both have δj=O⁡(p2​ν+2)\delta_{j}=O(p^{2\nu+2}). At each sufficiently small pp, at least one of the two syndromes therefore forces equal MAP decisions on its data endpoints, violating their required odd parity. In every case, each candidate syndrome has probability

Pr⁡(s∗(j))=2​F0​x​yκ−1+O⁡(pκ+1)=Θ⁡(pκ).\Pr(s_*^{(j)})=2F_{0}xy^{\kappa-1}+O(p^{\kappa+1})=\Theta(p^{\kappa}).

Each case therefore supplies a syndrome of probability Θ⁡(pκ)\Theta(p^{\kappa}) on which MAP is inconsistent, proving Pinc​(p)=Ω⁡(pκ)P_{\mathrm{inc}}(p)=\Omega(p^{\kappa}). In the balanced odd-degree case, the successful placement may depend on pp, but the constants are uniform over the two choices. No limit or expansion for q/pq/p is needed. ∎

Corollary 1 (Quartic inconsistency for the LP and Kasai code matrices).

For the LP code matrix with n=1122n=1122 and five noisy measurement rounds, and the Kasai code matrix with n=1152n=1152 and eight noisy measurement rounds, the independent X/ZX/Z phenomenological model with data-fault probability pp and measurement-fault probability q=Θ⁡(p)q=\Theta(p) has Pinc​(p)=Ω⁡(p4)P_{\mathrm{inc}}(p)=\Omega(p^{4}) under exact marginal MAP.

Proof.

The spatial checks provided in the Supplementary Information verify the hypotheses of Theorem 1. Both matrices have a minimum column degree ν=3\nu=3. At the selected qubit, the other degree-3 incidence counts are (4,4,4)(4,4,4) for LP and (11,11,11)(11,11,11) for Kasai, so NA=NBN_{A}=N_{B}. The measurement-round counts admit both placements. Direct enumeration in Supplementary Information confirms the separate data/measurement counts for each placement. ∎

All asymptotic statements hold at fixed code and measurement-round count. The theorem concerns exact marginals in the independent X/ZX/Z model. Approximate NeuralMP decoding and depolarizing simulations are assessed separately by their numerical results.

IV.4 Diversification

After iterative GNN decoding, almost all remaining failures leave a nonzero residual syndrome; syndrome-consistent but incorrect corrections are comparatively very rare. Similar cases arise in belief propagation and are commonly addressed by generating alternative decoding attempts and keeping the best consistent one [79, 43, 5]. We apply this principle to the trained NeuralMP: for shots whose residual syndrome remains nonzero, the network infers correction candidates with modified versions of the decoding problem and selects the one with the highest confidence.

Syndrome-flip (SF) search. We hypothesize a small set of error mechanisms, indicated by tt, and decode the modified syndrome s′=s⊕H​ts^{\prime}=s\oplus Ht with the same iterative NeuralMP, obtaining e′e^{\prime}. The candidate for the original problem is e=t⊕e′e=t\oplus e^{\prime}, which satisfies H​e=sHe=s whenever H​e′=s′He^{\prime}=s^{\prime}. Because the network re-decodes the modified syndrome, it can revise the whole correction rather than only the hypothesized bits. The hypotheses are guided by the network’s confidence through two signals: absz, which ranks mechanisms by the smallest absolute logit of the first iteration|z0,f||z_{0,f}| (locally ambiguous decisions), and flip, which ranks mechanisms by how often they are corrected across the iterations (decisions that are revised repeatedly, the neural analog of the oscillation signal of BP-SF [79]). For each signal we take the 32 top-ranked mechanisms and form 32 single, 32 pair and 32 triple hypotheses, giving 192 candidates per shot.

Further diversification. For LP20 Code, if all SF candidates have non-sero residual syndrome, a second stage decodes the syndrome in equivalent representations given by code automorphism (H​Pg=Dg​HHP_{g}=D_{g}H, Pg​p=pP_{g}p=p), for which the network is not exactly equivariant (because of positional encoding) and therefore follows different trajectories, combined with random multiplicative perturbations of the prior inputs, p~f=clip⁡(pf​eα​ξf)\tilde{p}_{f}=\mathrm{clip}(p_{f}e^{\alpha\xi_{f}}), ξf∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\xi_{f}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). After decoding, candidates are mapped back to the original coordinates.

Selection. Among candidates with H​e=sHe=s we select e⋆=arg⁡min​∑fef​log⁡1−pfpfe^{\star}=\arg\min\sum_{f}e_{f}\log\frac{1-p_{f}}{p_{f}} under the original noise model; if none is consistent, the output of the fourth iterative decoding is retained. No ground-truth information is used.

The search converts the dominant failure mode, non-convergence, into a recoverable one: for the Kasai code at p=1.5%p=1.5\% it resolves 99.6% of the shots left unresolved by iterative decoding, reducing the unresolved fraction from 2.6×10−42.6\times 10^{-4} to 1.0×10−61.0\times 10^{-6} per shot. Since these search methods have similar patterns, with the help of neutral network we can make candidates decoding as parallel batch, its latency can be amortized.

IV.5 Quantum memory benchmarks

For LP20 code, we simulate r=5r=5 measurement rounds with independent XX and ZZ data errors, each occurring with a probability pp, and measurement errors occurring with a probability q=pq=p. For Kasai, we use r=8r=8 measurement rounds with depolarizing data errors of probability pp and measurement errors of probability q=4​p/3q=4p/3.

For LP20 code, we set the hidden dimension of NeuralMP as χ=128\chi=128 and 12 MP-rounds; for Kasai code, the network has a hidden dimension of χ=64\chi=64 and 80 MP-rounds. Both use at most four outer iterations. Shots with a nonzero residual enter syndrome-flip search, which tests 192 iterative-decoding candidates constructed using uncertainty and repeated-correction signals. For LP20 code, shots without a syndrome-consistent candidate enter an additional stage of 396 prior-perturbed, symmetry-transformed candidates and 96 syndrome-flip candidates guided by symmetry-view disagreement. And for the Kasai code, Triage uses no second search stage. Candidates are checked against the original syndrome and ranked using the original noise priors.

For LP20 code, BP-OSD baseline uses 100 min-sum iterations with scaling 0.625 and order-10 combination-sweep OSD. Its relay-BP baseline uses 100 initial BP iterations and up to 300 relay stages of 60 iterations each. For Kasai code, the two-stage baseline uses 100 min-sum iterations followed by up to 300 relay stages of 60 iterations; Tiered adds a COPT-based search, with a limit of 120 seconds per side and eight solver threads.

The per-qubit-per-round LER is [1−(1−P¯)1/r]/k[1-(1-\bar{P})^{1/r}]/k, where P¯\bar{P} is the mean of the block failure probabilities for the two logical sectors and kk is the number of logical qubits. Error bars combine 95% Clopper–Pearson intervals with uncertainty in the sector when the failed sector was not recorded; treating sector counts as independent in the interval calculation is an approximation.

For Triage, the plotted amortized time uses a batch size of 64 and combines measured front-end and search costs with observed search frequencies, including handoff and final processing. The neural decoder was measured on one NVIDIA H-series GPU; the algorithmic baselines were measured on the CPU, with single-threaded BP and relay-BP and eight threads for the Tiered solver.
